items.title: Formalizing US Tax Code (Using Lean)
items.content:
Yesterday, we verified that known tax loopholes could be identified using a Lean search. Today, we set out to formalize the entire Internal Revenue Code to hunt for unknown loopholes (bugs).

Pointing a proof checker at statutes

Lean is a programming language whose type checker can also check mathematical proofs: if Lean accepts a proof, every step follows from the definitions, with nothing taken on trust. An earlier post discussed how far that kind of formalisation can reach in law, and yesterday we used it on the retirement-account rules, where a blind search rediscovered the backdoor Roth.

This work is part of , a CC0 repository of versioned legislation and case law. Our argument is that pointing AI and a proof checker at a versioned record of the law finds the contradictions and mechanical mistakes that people miss. In particular, we can catch mistakes in the text, and see what the rules allow, including what they allow by accident. To do so, we translated each section of the law into Lean, staying close to the statute’s own words, and tested it against the worked examples the IRS prints in its forms and instructions.

1. The tax law’s text has 138 drafting mistakes

The tax law is Title 26 of the US Code. Its official text is published as structured data by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, the office of the House of Representatives that compiles the Code.We used the release current to 3 November 2026.

A parser then reads every cross-reference, including the ones written in words (“paragraph (2) of subsection (b)”, “such subparagraph”, “sections 922 through 927”), which carry no hyperlink. Lean checks each one. Does the provision it points to exist? Is it still in force? (verifiable via our versioned history) The checks run as a test suite, which fails whenever a new release adds a fault the last one did not have.

The suite reports 257 findings, each checked by an AI agent against the official text and its editorial notes: 98 intended (rules for past periods, and provisions enacted but not yet in effect), 21 false alarms in the editors’ own hyperlinks, and 138 real faults:

Each of the 138 has a certificate: a short Lean statement that carries its evidence from the official XML and proves the fault. For a dead reference, the evidence is the full list of what does exist under the cited provision. Lean re-checks all 138 in about two and a half minutes.

Our record of the US Code is a git history, one commit per public law, so each fault can be traced to the law that wrote it. For Title 26 the record reaches back to the 1994 edition.

This check is cheap to repeat. Run against each new release of the Code, it flags a new mistake as soon as it appears, and names the law that caused it.

2. Rewriting the income tax as code that can be checked

Next we wrote down what the law calculates: the 2025 federal income tax for one household, meaning the numbers on Form 1040, including the changes made by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025. We did it in four parts:

  • , down to adjusted gross income (AGI). AGI is total income minus a few items, such as IRA contributions and student-loan interest. Most other tax rules depend on it.
  • : the standard deduction or itemized deductions, and the new deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest and people over 65.
  • , including the alternative minimum tax (AMT), a second calculation that stops high earners from cutting their tax too far with deductions.
  • , such as the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit (EITC), a credit for people on low and moderate wages.

We used AI to translate the statute into Lean. This is the lossy step, therefore we reinforce it with the following measures:

  • Each part is tested against figures the IRS publishes (the Tax Table, the EITC table, the worksheets and the examples in its publications), and checked against three independent tax programs on 5,000 households (section 3).
  • A second agent, which did not write that part, reviews it adversarially, looking for errors and for cheating, such as code written to pass the tests rather than to follow the statute.

What Lean ultimately adds is proofs that cover every input instead of a sample. For example, it proves that the SALT cap and the car-loan and overtime deductions never grow when income rises, at every income and for every filing status.

The comparison with other tax software helps us catch logical errors. That is how we caught two mistakes in our own model. It is also how we found bugs in the other tools that were logical rather than arithmetic: Tax-Calculator gives the EITC to separate filers without checking whether the spouses lived apart, and UsTaxes never attaches Schedule C to the 2025 return, so self-employment income disappears.

Writing the model turned up five things:

  • The published Code mixes 2025 and 2026 law. In six places the consolidated Code already shows the 2025 Act’s amendments that start in 2026. Read without the effective-date notes, it gives the wrong 2025 tax: the AMT phase-out at 50% instead of 25%, a charity floor and a cap on itemized deductions that do not yet apply.
  • The same Act rounds in opposite directions. The new tips and overtime deductions shrink by $100 for each full $1,000 of income over the limit, so one more dollar of income can cost $100 of deduction. The new car-loan deduction shrinks by $200 for each $1,000 “or portion thereof”, which rounds the other way, so it runs out $999 sooner than the round numbers suggest.
  • A married couple can deduct more state and local tax by filing separately. The deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) is capped, and the cap shrinks as income rises: by 30 cents for each dollar over $500,000 on a joint return. On a separate return, the law halves the cap after shrinking it, so it shrinks by only 15 cents a dollar. A couple earning $300,000 each can deduct up to $25,000 on two separate returns, but only $10,000 on one joint return.
  • The Tax Table is not the tax formula. Most people with taxable income under $100,000 look up their tax in the IRS Tax Table instead of working it out. The table differs from the formula in the law by between −$5 and +$6, and Lean proves that range for every income under $100,000 and every filing status.
  • One dollar can cost $8,046. Some benefits switch off at a line instead of fading out. A family with three children can lose its whole EITC, up to $8,046, because its investment income is one dollar over $11,950. The saver’s credit, a credit for retirement saving, works the same way: a couple who each put $2,000 into retirement accounts gets $2,000 at an income of $47,500, and $800 at $47,501.

3. Testing it against tax software people already use

A model is only useful if it gives the right answers. To check ours, we built 5,000 sample households and worked out each one’s 2025 tax four ways: with our model, and with three tools built by other teams, independently of each other and of us:

  • , an open-source model that researchers and policymakers use to estimate how tax and benefit changes affect households;
  • , the Policy Simulation Library’s open-source model of the federal income tax;
  • , a free, open-source app for preparing your own tax return.

Two thousand households were ordinary. The other 3,000 were deliberately awkward: couples filing separately, widows and widowers, students, people with tips or overtime, IRAs and health savings accounts, education and saver’s credits, and incomes over $1 million with large investment gains.

Our model and PolicyEngine-US agreed on every figure for 4,993 of the 5,000 households. The other seven differ by at most $11, all in the EITC: our model reads the IRS’s printed EITC table, while PolicyEngine-US uses the formula behind it.

gave the EITC and the child and dependent care credit to married people filing separately without checking that the spouses lived apart, which the law requires. It also computed no AMT for one high-earning separate filer, where two other calculators computed $14,881.

had 14 bugs, each confirmed by recalculating an affected household. It drops self-employment income without a warning, because its 2025 return never attaches Schedule C, the form for business income. Its child-care credit never reaches the return. Its age test for the EITC always passes. And its self-employment tax counts a spouse’s wages against the cap on Social Security tax. Together, these bugs affect about one ordinary household in six.

The comparison caught two mistakes in our own model too. We had not counted self-employment profit toward the 20% deduction for small-business income. And we always took the larger of the standard and itemized deductions, although the law lets you choose to itemize a smaller amount, which can pay when it lowers the AMT. With that fixed, one household owed $2,070 less. Both mistakes showed up because two independent tools agreed with each other and not with us.

4. A search found the loopholes tax advisers already use

With a model that matches the reference software, we used it as we had used the retirement rules: as the oracle for a search that knows no tax planning. The first search tried ordinary choices for each of the 5,000 households, 195,787 returns in all:

  • file separately, and which spouse holds which investments, pays which bills and claims which children;
  • realize more or less gain.

The second search used a multi-year family model, which adds the kiddie tax, trust taxation, Roth conversions, required withdrawals, gifts and death. It tried about 30,000 plans for four families over 34 to 47 years. Everything large that the two searches found is already in the planning literature:

A business owner files separately to get under the §199A threshold
The lower earner claims the children on a separate return
Realize less gain to stay under the EITC investment limit$6,798 for $5,000 deferred
Itemize a smaller amount to cut the AMT
Roth conversions in the gap years before Social Security
Pay your children wages, and open Roth IRAs for them
Convert so the heirs do not stack ten-year withdrawalsJournal of Accountancy

As with the backdoor Roth, none of these was described to the search. It found them because the rules, written down plainly, permit them.

5. Novel loopholes we found

Three results did not turn up in practitioner sources, IRS guidance or tax-software forums.

Filing separately can cut tax on Social Security, even for a couple living together. The standard advice is that a couple living together should never file separately when one draws Social Security. A separate filer who lived with their spouse gets no base amount at all. But taxable benefits are capped at the lesser of 85% of benefits or 85% of provisional income, and the search found couples for whom that cap makes separate returns cheaper. On a joint return the working spouse’s wage counts in provisional income, so a moderate wage already pushes the benefits to the 85% maximum. On a separate return the retiree’s benefits are measured against the retiree’s income alone. With $48,000 of benefits and a $60,000 wage, the couple owes $7,050 jointly and $5,568 separately, $1,482 less. A second reviewer recomputed it by hand and got the same answer. At a $100,000 wage the result flips, so the window is real but narrow.

Wages on one return, investments on the other. The 3.8% tax on investment income applies to the smaller of the investment income and the excess of income over $250,000 jointly, or $125,000 on a separate return. On a joint return, wages use up that threshold first. On separate returns the investing spouse’s income excludes the other’s wages, and their gains start in their own 0% band. With about $200,000 of each, that saves $1,621. Every explainer gives the threshold. We found none that describes the split or where it pays.

Schedule 8812 pays more than the statute allows. This is a gap between the IRS form and the law, not a plan. The statute caps the refundable child credit per qualifying child, computed without the $500 credit for other dependents. The form caps the combined credit instead, so in the phase-out range, with no tax left to absorb it, it refunds the $500 credits in cash. Example: one child and one other dependent, $240,000 of income, no tax left. The statute gives $200, the form $700. Lean proves the form is never below the statute and agrees with it exactly when there are no other dependents.

6. Why one year of the tax code holds no big loopholes

The backdoor Roth is big because two provisions combine to remove an income limit entirely, and the money then compounds tax-free for decades. A single year of the individual income tax is full of cliffs and per-return thresholds, but each is bounded: the largest swing we found was a few thousand dollars. Over decades, the large gains come from moves that are already published. The one combination we could not find written up was paying the children in the same years as Roth conversions, which adds about 0.5%. Our guess is that anything Roth-sized and unpublished lives where value moves between entities and their owners: partnerships, S corporations and C corporations.

7. Most of this can now run automatically

“The long-term problem is how this kind of bug-hunting can be done routinely, e.g. as part of a test suite. Some approaches aren’t really automatable, because they require a lot of both human and AI agent work.”

What still needs a person is deciding what a finding means. Some cliffs are deliberate. Others are in the IRS’s forms, not in the law, whilst others come from the way the official text is compiled, yet:

  • The text checks are routine. A new release is one download and one command, which fails on any fault the last release did not have, and git blame names the Act responsible.
  • The model is a one-off cost. Once written and proved, it is a build: if a later change breaks a proved property, the build fails. When the law changes, only the changed provisions need rewriting.
  • The comparison is routine once the input mappings are right. Getting them right was the hard part, and the same comparison found every mapping error.
  • The model covers the 2025 individual income tax for a household record. It leaves out the kiddie tax on the single-year return, 28% and §1250 gain, foreign income, passive activity rules, and most AMT preferences. The multi-year model holds 2025 law constant.
  • The drafting triage and the reviews were done by AI agents against the official text, and have not been checked by a lawyer or CPA.
  • Where all four calculators agree they may share a misreading. The theorems and the IRS-example tests are the check on the model itself.

The code, the certificates, the comparison and the searches are in the lean-proofs folder of global-law.

Serving GLM-5.3 at 607.8 tok/s across two Nvidia DGX stations with vLLM
items.content:
Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. 

The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

  • SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the DGX Station software stack. Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories.
  • At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files.
  • A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated cais/hle dataset: sign in, open its page, and select Agree and access repository. Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset.

The companion video follows the same workflow.

Step 1. Prepare the two Stations

This tutorial uses a separate computer, such as your laptop, to manage both Stations. Start by opening an SSH session to each Station from that computer. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. Run every command in this step on both Stations unless it starts with “On A.”

The two Stations run the same container and checkpoint in different roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the API, and Station B (rank 1) runs only a worker, with no API server.

First, check Docker access and collect the network values you’ll use later:

docker version
ibdev2netdev
ip -br addr

The output lists the two direct rails, and . Pick one for serving traffic, for example , and note two things for it on each Station:

  • , on the line that ends with the rail’s name. In mlx5_1 port 1 ==> cx8r1 (Up), the device is .
  • , on the line that starts with the rail’s name. In cx8r1 UP 192.168.101.1/24, the address is .

The rail name and device are the same on both Stations; only the IPv4 address differs.

Next, create on each Station. This file stores the values that later commands use:

Paste the following block and replace each placeholder, keeping the quotes, with the values you noted.

RANK="<NODE_RANK>"                    # RANK="0" on Station A, RANK="1" on Station B 
HEAD_IP="<STATION_A_IPV4_ADDRESS>"    # IPv4 address you noted on Station A; same in both files
WORKER_IP="<STATION_B_IPV4_ADDRESS>"  # IPv4 address you noted on Station B; same in both files
RAIL_IFACE="<RAIL_NAME>"              # Rail you picked, for example cx8r1; same in both files
RAIL_HCA="<RDMA_DEVICE>"              # RDMA device you noted, for example mlx5_1; same in both files

IMG=vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0-aarch64
IMG+=@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56
MODEL_REPO=nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
MODEL_REV=e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf
MODEL_HOST="$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4"
CONTAINER=glm53-full
PORT=8000

if [ "$RANK" = 0 ]; then
  NODE_IP=$HEAD_IP; PEER_IP=$WORKER_IP
else
  NODE_IP=$WORKER_IP; PEER_IP=$HEAD_IP
fi

GPU_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --format=csv,noheader |
  awk -F, '$2 ~ /GB300/ {gsub(/ /,"",$1); print $1; exit}')

For example, with the default addresses on , Station A’s file starts like this. Station B’s file is identical except for :

RANK="0"
HEAD_IP="192.168.101.1"
WORKER_IP="192.168.101.2"
RAIL_IFACE="cx8r1"
RAIL_HCA="mlx5_1"

is built from your home directory, and Step 2 copies the checkpoint over SSH to the same path on Station B.

On both Stations, load the values and check storage, connectivity, and baseline memory:

source ~/glm53.env
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST" && df -h "$MODEL_HOST"
ethtool "$RAIL_IFACE"
ip link show dev "$RAIL_IFACE"
ping -I "$RAIL_IFACE" -M do -s 8972 -c 3 "$PEER_IP"
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
nvidia-smi

These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes before they surface as NCCL timeouts. Expect a link, MTU 9000, successful jumbo-frame pings, and synchronized time. should show no compute processes on the GB300. On a Station with a display GPU, Xorg can appear on both GPUs with a few MiB.

Step 2 copies the checkpoint from A to B over SSH, so A needs passwordless access to B. On A, create a key without a passphrase (see SSH keys for details), copy its public key to B after checking B’s host fingerprint, and confirm the login: 

ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id "$WORKER_IP"
ssh -o BatchMode=yes "$WORKER_IP" hostname

Step 2. Download and copy the model

Tensor parallelism requires both ranks to run the same software against the same weights. Start by pulling the pinned image on both Stations:

docker pull "$IMG" &&
docker image inspect "$IMG" --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'

The pull can take several minutes. Matching arm64 digests mean both ranks run identical software.

On A, download the pinned checkpoint. At about 464 GB, it takes roughly an hour at 1 Gb/s, or about six minutes at 10 Gb/s:

mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST"
docker run --rm --network host -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model" \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc \
  "exec hf download '$MODEL_REPO' --revision '$MODEL_REV' --local-dir /model"

When prints , copy the files to B. On A:

ssh "$WORKER_IP" "mkdir -p '$MODEL_HOST'" &&
rsync -aH --info=progress2 --exclude '.cache/' \
  "$MODEL_HOST/" "$WORKER_IP:$MODEL_HOST/"

Each disk keeps the full checkpoint; vLLM partitions the weights across the GPUs at load time, with no further quantization.

On A, compare both copies (the check reads B’s file list over SSH), then validate the checkpoint:

(
  set -euo pipefail
  L=$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -path '*/.cache' -prune -o \
    -type f -printf '%P %s\n' | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum)
  R=$(ssh "$WORKER_IP" "set -o pipefail; find '$MODEL_HOST' \
    -path '*/.cache' -prune -o -type f -printf '%P %s\\n' | \
    LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum")
  test "$L" = "$R"
  test "$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -maxdepth 1 \
    -name 'model-*-of-00050.safetensors' | wc -l)" = 50
  python3 -c "import json; c=json.load(open('$MODEL_HOST/config.json')); \
assert c['architectures']==['GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM']; \
assert c['quantization_config']['quant_algo']=='MIXED_PRECISION'"
  echo MODEL_READY
)

means both Stations hold the same file names and sizes in the expected layout. is expected: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor.

Step 3. Launch the distributed service

This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads , and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: , the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.

On both Stations, create a file named :

The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several tokens. The gain depends on how often drafts are accepted, which varies with the prompt.

FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens. Prefix caching is enabled to avoid reprocessing prompt prefixes the server has already seen. Paste the script below; it checks your configuration, finds the RoCE GID index for the selected rail, and starts this Station’s vLLM rank in a container:

set -euo pipefail
source "$HOME/glm53.env"
case "$RANK" in 0|1) ;; *) echo "Invalid RANK" >&2; exit 1;; esac
test -n "$GPU_UUID"
test -f "$MODEL_HOST/config.json"
GID_INDEX=$(/usr/sbin/show_gids 2>/dev/null |
  awk -v d="$RAIL_HCA" -v ip="$NODE_IP" \
  '$1==d && $5==ip && $6=="v2" {g=$3} END {if(g!="") print g}')
test -n "$GID_INDEX"
HEADLESS=
if [ "$RANK" = 1 ]; then HEADLESS=--headless; fi
SPEC_CONFIG='{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'
KERNEL_CONFIG='{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false,"moe_backend":"flashinfer_cutlass"}'
COMPILE_CONFIG='{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,10,20,40,80],"pass_config":{"fuse_allreduce_rms":false}}'

docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --gpus device="$GPU_UUID" --network host --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  --device /dev/infiniband --cap-add IPC_LOCK \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model:ro" \
  -e RANK="$RANK" -e HEADLESS="$HEADLESS" \
  -e MASTER_ADDR="$HEAD_IP" -e MODEL_REPO="$MODEL_REPO" -e PORT="$PORT" \
  -e SPEC_CONFIG="$SPEC_CONFIG" -e KERNEL_CONFIG="$KERNEL_CONFIG" \
  -e COMPILE_CONFIG="$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
  -e NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1 -e NCCL_IB_HCA="$RAIL_HCA" \
  -e NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX="$GID_INDEX" \
  -e NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 -e NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7 \
  -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0 -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM=0 \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" \
  -e NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 -e NCCL_DEBUG=INFO -e NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET \
  -e NCCL_DEBUG_FILE='/tmp/nccl_%h_%p.log' -e VLLM_HOST_IP="$NODE_IP" \
  -e VLLM_EXECUTE_MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800 \
  -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  -e VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 -e FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc '
    set -euo pipefail  
    # Use NCCL 2.30.7 from the image: older versions can deadlock
    # cross-node CUDA graph replays over RoCE (vLLM issue #52504).
    export VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH=$(python3 -c "import nvidia.nccl,os;
print(os.path.join(list(nvidia.nccl.__path__)[0], \"lib\", \"libnccl.so.2\"))")
    test -f "$VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH"
    EXTRA=()
    if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then EXTRA+=("$HEADLESS"); fi
    exec vllm serve /model --served-model-name "$MODEL_REPO" \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port "$PORT" \
      --nnodes 2 --node-rank "$RANK" --master-addr "$MASTER_ADDR" \
      --master-port 29501 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
      --speculative-config "$SPEC_CONFIG" \
      --max-model-len 98304  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
      --block-size 128 --max-num-seqs 16 \
      --trust-remote-code --disable-custom-all-reduce \
      --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 \
      --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
      --kernel-config "$KERNEL_CONFIG" --compilation-config "$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
      --distributed-timeout-seconds 1800 \
      --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm47 \
      "${EXTRA[@]}"
  '

Run the script on B first, then on A:

Each command prints a container ID and returns immediately; the service is not ready yet. B’s worker waits for A to join, then each Station loads its share of the weights from local storage, prepares kernels, and captures CUDA graphs. This takes several minutes.

On A, follow the log to see when the service is ready ( hides output from earlier runs):

docker logs --follow --since "$(docker inspect \
  --format '{{.State.StartedAt}}' "$CONTAINER")" "$CONTAINER"

When the log shows Application startup complete, press Ctrl+C to stop following it; the service keeps running.

At this point one model spans two machines. Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.

The remaining GPU memory holds the KV cache, which stores the context of in-flight requests. The startup log reports its capacity (GPU KV cache size). All requests in flight share it, so longer prompts or more users need more of it. If you run out, lower or send fewer requests at once.

Step 4. Verify serving and send a request

On A, check the API ( is A itself):

docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 10 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null && echo HEALTH_OK

proves that Station A answers. Next, on both Stations, check that the ranks communicate over GPU RDMA rather than falling back to TCP sockets. The check reads the NCCL logs that the launcher writes through , and the same block shows the loaded memory:

docker exec "$CONTAINER" bash -lc '
  set -euo pipefail
  files=(/tmp/nccl_*.log)
  test -e "${files[0]}"
  grep -hE "NET/IB.*GDRDMA|GPU Direct RDMA Enabled" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  grep -hF "$NCCL_IB_HCA" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  if grep -hE "NET/Socket|NCCL WARN|NCCL ERROR" "${files[@]}"; then
    exit 1
  fi
  echo RDMA_CHECK_OK
'
nvidia-smi

means the check passed with no warnings. In , A shows the process and B shows , one rank per GPU. The startup log reports about 218 GiB of weights per GPU, roughly half the checkpoint, which confirms that the model is split across the two GPUs.

On A, send a chat request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 120 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Quarterly units sold: Q1 = 120; Q2 = 180; Q3 = 150. Summarize the trend in one sentence and calculate the percentage change from Q1 to Q2."}],
    "temperature":0,"max_tokens":4096,
    "chat_template_kwargs":{"reasoning_effort":"low"}}' |
python3 -c 'import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin)["choices"][0];
print(c["message"]["content"]); print("finish_reason:",c["finish_reason"])'

The response should look like this:

**Trend:** Units sold rose sharply in Q2 before partially declining in Q3, remaining above the Q1 level.

**Q1 → Q2 percentage change:** (180 - 120) / 120 × 100 = **50% increase**
finish_reason: stop

means the model finished its answer instead of hitting the token limit. The request sets to in . GLM-5.3 also accepts and , which let it reason longer before answering, at the cost of latency. Because the launcher enables tool calling (--enable-auto-tool-choice), agent frameworks that use the OpenAI tools API can call the same endpoint.

Step 5. Concurrency and release resources

AIPerf, the NVIDIA benchmarking tool for inference endpoints, measures throughput and latency. Installing it inside the serving container can change vLLM’s dependencies, so on A, install it in its own virtual environment:

sudo apt update &&
sudo apt install -y python3.12-venv python3.12-dev build-essential &&
python3.12 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0" &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" install 'aiperf==0.12.0' &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" check

The install should end with No broken requirements found.

AIPerf can send synthetic prompts or replay an existing dataset. This tutorial uses the 80 Coding conversations from SPEED-Bench, a set of real prompts built to evaluate speculative decoding, so MTP is measured on realistic text. SPEED-Bench’s preparation script fetches these prompts from several Hugging Face datasets, including the gated cais/hle: if you haven’t already, open its page and select Agree and access repository before you continue. Then, on A, log in to Hugging Face:

"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/hf" auth login

SPEED_BENCH_DIR="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench"
mkdir -p "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
curl -fLsS https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Skills/refs/heads/main/nemo_skills/dataset/speed-bench/prepare.py | \
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - --config qualitative --output_dir "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"

On A, check the dataset and service. Continue when the check prints :

(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  curl -fsS "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/health" >/dev/null
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - <<'PY_CHECK'
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path.home()
path = root / "datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
assert path.exists(), "Dataset missing: rerun the SPEED-Bench preparation"
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
coding = [row for row in rows if row["category"] == "coding"]
assert len(coding) == 80, "Expected 80 Coding conversations"
assert sum(len(row["messages"]) for row in coding) == 89
assert all("FULL BENCHMARK DATA SHOULD BE FETCHED" not in message["content"]
           for row in coding for message in row["messages"])
print("BENCHMARK_READY: dataset has 80 Coding conversations, 89 turns in total.")

PY_CHECK
)

The full sweep covers concurrency 1, 8, 16, and 32. At each level, AIPerf sends 3×C warmup requests, then measures 10×C requests, where C is the concurrency. Some conversations are sent more than once at higher concurrency.

Benchmark requests use the model’s default reasoning effort (max) and an 8,192-token output cap; responses can finish before reaching it. Full sweeps can take several hours.

 A two-hour request timeout leaves room for long responses, collects server counters used to measure MTP acceptance, and keeps each response for inspection. 

For a quick test, run the block below on A with both containers running and no other API traffic. It tests C1 and C8 with prefix caching enabled, as in the reference measurements in Table 2, below.

(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  CODING_DATASET="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
  test -f "$CODING_DATASET"
 export CONCURRENCIES=${CONCURRENCIES:-"1 8"} # Quick run: C1 and C8.
  # Optional full benchmark: follow the reproduction instructions below.
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 16 -> export CONCURRENCIES="1 8 16"
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 32 -> export CONCURRENCIES=32

  RUN_DIR="$HOME/aiperf-results/blog-coding-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
  for C in $CONCURRENCIES;  do
    ART="$RUN_DIR/c$C"
    env -u HF_HUB_OFFLINE -u TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE \
      "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/aiperf" profile \
      -m "$MODEL_REPO" --url "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT" \
      --endpoint-type chat --streaming --tokenizer "$MODEL_HOST" \
      --custom-dataset-type speed_bench_coding --input-file "$CODING_DATASET" \
      --request-count "$((10 * C))" --warmup-request-count "$((3 * C))" \
      --osl 8192 \
      --use-server-token-count --concurrency "$C" --random-seed 42 \
      --request-timeout-seconds 7200 \
      --server-metrics "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/metrics" \
      --export-level raw --artifact-dir "$ART"
    printf "Results: %s\n" "$ART"
  done
  printf "Results directory: %s\n" "$RUN_DIR"
)

AIPerf saves metrics, raw responses, and logs in the results directory. Warmup requests are excluded from the reported metrics.

Optional: Reproduce Table 2. In from Step 3 on both Stations, keep and set to 16 or 32 for the corresponding group shown in the comments above. Before each group, stop and remove the current containers on A, then B (docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER", followed by ). Relaunch the updated script on B, then A with bash and wait for Application startup complete. On A, run the matching command from the comments, then rerun the AIPerf block.

To test without prefix caching, replace with --no-enable-prefix-caching in the Step 3 script on both Stations, then recreate the containers as above. Performance may differ from Table 2.

Figure 2 compares overall output throughput across measured requests with mean per-user throughput. Token counts include reasoning.

Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.

Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32. 

After the requests finish, stop the vLLM container on A, then on B:

docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER"
docker inspect --format \
  'Status={{.State.Status}} Running={{.State.Running}}' "$CONTAINER"
nvidia-smi

The status should read Status=exited Running=false, with no vLLM processes in ; the checkpoint, containers, and results stay on disk. To resume, run docker start "$CONTAINER" on B, then A, and repeat the Step 4 checks.

  • Missing variables or SSH failure: after reconnecting; verify A-to-B key authentication and B’s fingerprint.
  • SPEED-Bench preparation fails with a gated-dataset error: sign in to Hugging Face with the same account, open the cais/hle page, select Agree and access repository, then rerun the preparation.
  • Startup or RDMA check failure: inspect on both nodes; verify the checkpoint and the GID, and rerun the playbook’s validation (script 07).

You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.

Connect your own application using the vLLM serving documentation, then rerun AIPerf with your prompts to find the concurrency that fits your workload. A frontier-scale model is now ready to build on, right from your desk.

items.content:
To try to answer this question, we’ll build a digital being with a simple brain, and watch it learn a new behavior.

In our previous article, we created a creature called a spark that could steer towards light. And we saw how small changes to its neural circuitry gave rise to very different behaviors.

Back then, we’d wired these circuits into the spark’s brain by hand. But now, we want it to learn the same behaviors .

After all, you didn’t come into this world knowing how to walk, talk or read. While some of your abilities, such as breathing or swallowing, are wired by evolution, you gained others through an arduous process of trial and error.

We want our spark to do the same. To give you an intuition for this learning process, we’re going to hand over the controls to you. to wire the spark’s brain.

But first, we need to tell you what you’ll be wiring. The spark’s brain has just four neurons — two neurons serving as its eyes, and two neurons that wiggle its flippers.

There are between neurons on the same side of its body, between neurons on opposite sides, and , which controls the spark’s speed when there’s no light.

So its brain wiring boils down to just three numbers — the strength of each kind of connection, and the drive.

Now let’s set this spark loose. Use the sliders below to wire its brain as it moves. We’ll keep score.

Your goal: Make the spark love the light by

Finding the right configuration takes a lot of trial and error. (If you get stuck, click the hint button above for a nudge in the right direction.)

Let’s visualize what you just did. To guide the spark to the light, you tweaked three numbers. We can represent these numbers as the three axes of a cube.

The payoff of this picture is that we can visualize your spark’s learning trajectory as a path within this cube.

To guide the spark, you probably nudged a slider one way, saw whether this made things better or worse, and then used this feedback to decide your next move.

Let’s distill this into a — a step-by-step procedure by which the spark can rewire its brain through practice.

Here’s how it’ll work: The spark gets many tries to steer towards the light. Before every trial, its brain wiring will change a little at random, just like you wiggled the sliders to and fro.

If the trial goes better than previous ones, then the spark gets a reward and its wiring shifts in the direction of this random change. And if the trial goes worse, the spark gets a punishment, and its wiring shifts the other way.

This isn’t that different from how you learned how to walk or ride a bike. Falling down was your punishment, and the thrill of balancing was your reward.

Can this simple algorithm help the spark find the light?

In the beginning, the spark is a novice, with a brain that’s wired together at random. Unsurprisingly, it doesn’t get very far.

The baby spark can spin in place, but it can’t yet move around. But it’s about to get better…

After 50 tries of this learning algorithm, our infant spark has taken its first steps. And while it won’t break any speed records, it’s now on the move…

After 250 tries, our juvenile spark has picked up speed. But it veers away from the light at the last moment.

After 500 tries, our adolescent spark boldly charges towards the light. But it hasn’t yet figured out how to slow down or stop.

After 2,000 tries, our spark is now an adult — an expert at seeking and following the light. It clings to the light and can turn on a dime. (Try moving the light to see the spark follow it.)

Like before, we can visualize this learning process as a path.

This isn’t a path through physical space. Instead, it’s a path through the space of possible brains. It shows how the spark’s brain changed as it learned.

Other novice sparks would start from different points, and they would each trace out their own learning trajectory.

This tangled web illustrates the learning paths of hundreds of novice sparks, each starting with a differently wired brain. As if by magic, all of these threads converge to the point marked .

The paths aren’t straight lines: Learning isn’t linear. There are setbacks, wrong turns and mistakes along the way. And it isn’t necessarily fast. Some of the learners took thousands of tries to reach their goal.

You’ll notice that the paths are all jittery. That’s because every step involves randomness. We can smooth out this jitter by averaging over many trajectories at every point, revealing a map of the flow of learning.

It’s worth taking a moment to appreciate how surprising this is — given enough tries, the same learning process turned every novice into an expert light seeker.

Of the myriad possible arrangements of this spark’s brain, only a tiny fraction generate the behavior that we want. There are far more ways to fail than to succeed.

And yet, you’ve just witnessed a small miracle. The spark navigated this labyrinth of dead ends and rewired its brain to find the light, guided by nothing but reward and punishment.

Learning doesn’t stop once you become an adult. We learn throughout our lives and adapt to changing circumstances.

Our sparks can do this too. For example, what if the light represents a harmful chemical or a dangerous predator instead of a food source?

The spark is now rewarded for rather than for seeking it, and this leads to new behaviors:

If the light is harmful, then becomes the worst strategy, and the sparks learn to (escape as fast as possible) or to (play dead).

If instead the spark is rewarded for approaching the light with high speed, then it learns to charge towards the light, i.e. to .

Much like a child learns from its environment, the spark can learn very different behaviors — fleeing, freezing, fighting or following the light — depending on how it’s rewarded.

You’ve now seen how a novice spark can rewire its brain and learn new behaviors through a process known as reinforcement learning.

Biological brains also learn through reinforcement. For example, baby songbirds learn to sing by babbling. They try out random variations of their song. If a variation gets closer to their memory of an adult’s song, they get a burst of dopamine (and if it gets further away, the dopamine dips). Guided by these rewards and punishments, they can recreate the song from memory, even with no teacher present!

Now, we do have to come clean about something. This spark’s brain had just four neurons and three numbers that determined how these neurons were connected. This simple structure allowed us to watch its brain learn in three dimensions.

Your brain has around 86 billion neurons and over a hundred trillion connections. The space of possible ways in which it could be wired is therefore unimaginably vast.

But while the details are much more complicated, the underlying idea is the same: Learning is how you navigate this vast internal space. And feedback is the compass that points the way.

Thanks for reading chapter two of Myriad, a series exploring how minds emerge from matter. Myriad is a collaboration between Arkarup Banerjee, a neuroscientist who studies behavior, and Aatish Bhatia, a physicist turned science journalist.

The sparks in this article are inspired by the work of the neuroscientist Valentino Braitenberg. We implemented their neural circuitry as follows:

where and are the left and right flipper speeds, and are the brightness levels at the left and right eyes, and are the and connection strengths between the eyes and the flippers, and is a that sets the spark’s speed when there is no light. is the ReLU function. The spark’s forward speed is the average of the two flipper speeds, and its turning speed is proportional to their difference.

There are three parameters in our simplified setup: and The spark learns values for these parameters using a version of the REINFORCE algorithm published by Ronald Williams in 1992.

Each trial, the parameters were wiggled by a small random amount and the spark moved for 500 time steps, starting from a random point on the edge of the arena. Its reward was the average brightness along its path.

This reward was then compared to a running average of recent rewards. If the spark did better than usual, its parameters were nudged in the direction of this random change. If it did worse, its parameters were nudged in the opposite direction. The size of the nudge was proportional to how much better (or worse) it did:

Here is the change in the three parameters, is the learning rate, is the random wiggle, and is how much better or worse than usual the spark did. We repeated this thousands of times.

items.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
items.content:
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough by hand to have opinions about this.

The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.

Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

  • Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
  • Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
  • Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
  • Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
  • Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.

The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:

The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:

And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:

Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:

Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:

The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.

The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.

Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:

The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the in ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.

Parts of this have been done before:

  • in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.
  • : framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.
  • The has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. and (, and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
  • terminals can outline whole input fields.

What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.

When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.

Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.

The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):

Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:

Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: placement, colors, blocks, junctions, halves, styles and live. cycles the stroke width, turns borders off so you can compare, and quits. Each view also has a matching flag (, and so on) if you want to start on it.

The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:

Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. and split, closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.

The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:

It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. to show and hide the boxes, and work the same as in the panes demo, and or lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the dependency.

I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.
